title: A Fly Finds Singing Crickets With Ears Half a Millimetre Apart
subject: tachinid fly

scenes.text: For this cricket, singing is suicide. The killer's a fly.
Ormia ochracea, the size of a housefly. It hunts male crickets by their chirps, in the dark.
Its ears sit half a millimetre apart, so a chirp reaches both almost together. The gap is about fifty billionths of a second.
Yet it pinpoints the singer to within two degrees. A tiny lever joins its eardrums and makes one side fire late.
It lands and drops live maggots on the cricket. They burrow in and eat it alive for about a week.
Engineers copied those ears for hearing aids. The crickets found a simpler fix: on one Hawaiian island, most males stopped singing.

description:
A parasitic fly, Ormia ochracea, finds male crickets by their song using ears only about half a millimetre apart.
Cornell researchers showed it locates a chirp to within 2 degrees from a time difference of roughly 50 nanoseconds, thanks to a lever-like bridge between its eardrums. Its larvae eat the cricket alive for about a week. On Kauai, most male crickets have evolved silent wings to escape it.
Would you rather be the cricket that sings or the one that stays quiet?
thumbnail_text: SING, AND THE FLY FINDS YOU
first_comment: Those silent Kauai crickets now sit next to the few males that still sing and grab the females that come. Which animal has the best hearing you know of?
